finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST /hooks/test sends a server-side HTTP POST to an attacker-chosen URL with no validation.
finding.source: req.body.callback (routes.js:20), attacker-controlled request body on a public, unauthenticated route (pub.post, routes.js:19)

trace.note: pub.post("/hooks/test") is registered on the public router with no auth middleware
req.body.callback is passed straight into axios.post as the URL
res.json returns r.status to the caller, so the attacker learns the HTTP status of the internal response

finding.guards_checked: No auth middleware on pub. No scheme, host, IP, or port allowlist. No DNS/IP re-check at connect time. Axios follows redirects by default, so a public URL can redirect to an internal address. Only the status code is returned, but it still acts as a reachability oracle for internal hosts, and the fixed POST body can trigger side effects on internal services.

verdict.guard_found: none. routes.js:19 registers pub.post("/hooks/test") with no middleware, and routes.js:20 passes req.body.callback directly to axios.post with no scheme, host, or IP check. The only middleware in the file, requireAdmin (routes.js:7-12), is applied to admin via admin.use at routes.js:12 and does not cover pub.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: routes.js:19 defines the unauthenticated pub.post route, routes.js:20 uses req.body.callback as the axios.post URL with no validation, and routes.js:21 returns the status. The only auth check in the file, requireAdmin at routes.js:12, applies to admin and not pub. The one caveat is that the directory contains only routes.js, so I could not see whether pub is mounted behind an auth wrapper elsewhere; within the code available, the route is public.

finding.claim: GET /diagnostics/fetch sends a server-side GET to an arbitrary URL from the query string with no validation. Reachable only by an admin session.

trace.note: admin.use(requireAdmin) applies the admin session check to every route on the admin router
req.query.url goes straight into axios.get; the response status is returned at routes.js:16

finding.guards_checked: requireAdmin session/role check (routes.js:7-12). No URL scheme, host, or IP allowlist; no private-range block; no redirect restriction. Exploitation requires an admin session. The router is mounted elsewhere, so confirm it is not exposed without its session middleware; that code is not in this directory. If a non-admin can reach it, this becomes the same severity as SSRF-1.

verdict.guard_found: routes.js:12 `admin.use(requireAdmin)` applies to every route on the admin router, and routes.js:8 returns 403 unless `req.session.role === "admin"`. This is a session/role gate, not a URL validation, so it does not close SSRF on its own. Its effect is on the source: the attacker must already hold an admin session.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (routes.js:7-8, 12, 14-16 match the claim), but the source `req.query.url` at routes.js:15 is reachable only after the admin role check at routes.js:8 and 12, so it is not controlled by an unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker. The finding is therefore refuted as a low-privilege SSRF; it remains an admin-only issue, and the mount point is irrelevant because `admin.use` at routes.js:12 applies regardless of where the router is mounted.
